{{Short description|Health survey in the United States}}
The '''National Health Interview Survey''' ('''NHIS''') is an annual, [[Cross-sectional study|cross-sectional survey]] intended to provide nationally representative estimates on a wide range of [[Health status indicators|health status]] and [[Utilization management|utilization]] measures among the nonmilitary, noninstitutionalized population of the United States.  Each annual data set can be used to examine the [[disease burden]] and access to care that individuals and families are currently experiencing in the United States.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

NHIS is designed by the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]]'s [[National Center for Health Statistics]] (NCHS) – the government agency tasked to monitor the population's [[Health status indicators|health status]] and [[Behavior change (public health)|behavior]] – and administered by the [[U.S. Census Bureau]].<ref name="cdc">{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/404.htm|title=NCHS – 404 Error – Resource Not Available|date=1 June 2019|website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>  NHIS has been administered since 1957, although the core content and [[questionnaires]] undergo major revisions every 10–15 years.<ref name="cdc_a">{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about_nhis.htm |title=NHIS – About the National Health Interview Survey |publisher=Cdc.gov |date= |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref>  NHIS allows both governmental and outside [[researchers]] to obtain estimates on a variety of health-related topics among either the entire nation or specific [[demographics|demographic groups]] of the population.  Also, since the [[Sample survey|survey design]] is [[Cross-sectional study|cross-sectional]] rather than [[Longitudinal study|longitudinal]], health information can be trended for [[Demographics|demographic groups]] and the country as a whole, but not for individuals or families.

== History ==
Authorized by the [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2031124/ National Health Survey Act] of 1956,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/series/sr_01/sr01_011acc.pdf |title=Vital and Health Statistics; Series 1, No. 11 (4/75) |date= |accessdate=2019-06-11}}</ref> the [[U.S. Public Health Service]] was tasked with implementing an annual survey to collect information on [[Morbidity#Morbidity|morbidities]] – physical or [[Mental health|mental]] conditions related to any [[illness]] or [[injury]] – and medical service and [[medical facility]] utilization.  The most recent re-design of the survey [[questionnaire]] was implemented in 1997.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

== Research topics ==
[[File:Medical debt in USA. National Health Interview Survey.gif|thumb|Percentages of persons in families with selected financial burdens of medical care: United States, January–June 2011. Chart from "Financial Burden of Medical Care: Early Release of Estimates From the National Health Interview Survey".]]
NHIS data contain information on [[health]], [[Behavior change (public health)|influences on health]], and [[Outcomes research|health outcomes]], as well as common [[Demographics|demographic]] indicators to give users the ability to examine [[Health status indicators|health status]], [[Behavior change (public health)|behavior]], and [[risk factors]] within and across subsets of the population (such as racial and ethnic [[health disparities]]).{{cn|date=March 2024}}

The major health topics covered in the Core questionnaires include [[Health status indicators|health status]], [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|insurance coverage]], [[Alternative medicine|complementary and alternative medicine]], use of health services, [[immunizations]], [[Behavior change (public health)|health behaviors]], [[injuries]], [[occupational health]], [[cancer screening]], ability to perform daily activities, and conditions such as [[Behavior change (public health)|asthma]], [[Behavior change (public health)|diabetes]], [[Behavior change (public health)|mental health]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/factsheets/factsheet_nhis.htm |title=About NCHS – NCHS Fact Sheets – National Health Interview Survey |publisher=Cdc.gov |date=2013-07-11 |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref>  [[National Center for Health Statistics|NCHS]] continually produces chart books, statistical briefs, and fact sheets using NHIS data which shed light on these various facets of [[Morbidity#Morbidity|morbidities]] and how the American populace behaves in response.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

Periodically, the NHIS includes supplemental questionnaires regarding a focused topic that might be of particular current interest. For example, a [[cancer]] supplement was fielded in 1987, 1992, 2000, 2003, 2005, 2008, and 2010, and sponsored by the [[National Cancer Institute]] and the [https://www.cdc.gov/nccdphp/ National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention]. This supplement included questions about [[cancer screening]]s, [[diet (nutrition)|diet]], [[exercise]], [[smoking]], [[Health effects of sun exposure|sun exposure]], and [[Family history (medicine)|family history]].<ref name="cdc" />

Occupational supplement were fielded in 2010 and 2015, and sponsored by the [[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] (NIOSH). These supplement included questions about [[occupational injury|work-related health conditions]], work organization factors, and occupational psychosocial and physical/chemical exposures.<ref name = nhis_supplement>{{cite web|title=CDC – The 2010 Occupational Health Supplement to the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) Home Page – NIOSH Workplace Safety and Health Topic| publisher=National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | date=June 28, 2013|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/nhis|accessdate = July 16, 2013}}</ref>

== Publications ==
The National Health Interview Survey is commonly the subject of analysis in articles on [[Health status indicators|health status]] and health behaviors in research journals such as Obesity, Journal of the American Dietetic Association, Health Services Research, and the American Journal of Public Health.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&q='national+health+interview+survey'+'health+behavior'|title=Google Scholar|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

A number of CDC reports, including [https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/healthy_people.htm Healthy People], rely on NHIS to monitor health estimates.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

The [[Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)]], Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE) tracks health insurance coverage in the United States using the NHIS.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aspe.hhs.gov/insurance/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051113013046/http://aspe.hhs.gov/insurance/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 13, 2005 |title=Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, HHS: Health Insurance Data |publisher=Aspe.hhs.gov |date= |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref>

The National Center for Health Statistics publishes periodical statistical summaries,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/series/series10.htm |title=Products – Series Reports – Series 10 |publisher=Cdc.gov |date=2013-05-21 |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref> compiling the results of the most recent NHIS and trending those statistics over time for certain groups.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

NCHS/CDC also publish statistical reports on current topics of interest,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/nhsr.htm |title=Products – NHSR – Homepage |publisher=Cdc.gov |date= |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref> and shorter data briefs.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs.htm |title=Products – Data Briefs – Homepage |publisher=Cdc.gov |date=2013-09-18 |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref> For example, NIOSH has published several peer-reviewed journal articles from the 2010 and 2015 NHIS Occupational Health Supplement results.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/nhis/output.html|title=CDC – NHIS Publications and Resources Page – NIOSH Workplace Safety and Health Topic|date=6 March 2019|website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>

== Methodology ==

=== Survey design ===
Noninstitutional civilian Americans (both citizens and non-citizens) are sampled by [[household]], allowing for analysis of medical behavior at the familial-level.  After a household has been sampled, one adult and one child (if any are present) is selected to complete the Sample Adult and Sample Child components of the survey.  In years without budget cuts, approximately 35,000 households containing 87,500 individuals are included.<ref name="cdc_a" />

NHIS follows a multi-stage area probability design, meaning that geographic areas – rather than unique households – are sampled first, and then within those selected areas, residences are sampled.  Unlike surveys with a [[Longitudinal study|panel or longitudinal design]], the entirety of data collected from each household occurs from a single interview lasting about an hour.<ref name="cdc_a" />

The complex survey design must be analyzed with software capable of handling survey data that was not obtained from a [[simple random sample]], such as [[R (software)|R]], SUDAAN, [[SAS (software)|SAS]], [[Stata]], [[SPSS]], and VPLX.  In addition to appropriately weighting households that might have been over-represented in the raw data (due to oversampling of populations of interest), survey analysis packages are needed to employ the Taylor-series linearization technique to correctly calculate the [[standard error (statistics)|standard error]]s and [[confidence interval]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhis/2006var.pdf |title=Data |date=2006 |website=www.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

=== Linkage to other health surveys ===
The [[Medical Expenditure Panel Survey]] currently uses the NHIS sampled population to form its own sampling frame (ultimately sampling one-half of NHIS respondent households for its own publicly available complete survey).<ref name="cdc_a" />  After filling out a confidentiality agreement, AHRQ provides a crosswalk to merge these data.<ref>{{cite web|author=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality |url=http://www.meps.ahrq.gov/mepsweb/data_stats/more_info_download_data_files.jsp#hc-nhis |title=Medical Expenditure Panel Survey Data File Types |publisher=Meps.ahrq.gov |date=2006-01-08 |accessdate=2013-10-13}}</ref>

NHIS data can also be linked to death certificates in the [https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/ndi.htm National Death Index (NDI)].

== Data Available ==

NHIS data are freely downloadable by the public, and generally become available in June or July for the preceding year's data set.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/data-questionnaires-documentation.htm|title=NHIS – Data, Questionnaires and Related Documentation|date=23 May 2019|website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>  Certain variables that might make survey respondents easily identifiable (such as geographic locations, exact dates of events and procedures) are not available from the publicly available data, but can be accessed and analyzed by applying for access to the NCHS [https://www.cdc.gov/rdc/ Research Data Center].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/rdc/b1datatype/Dt100.htm|title=RDC – Types of Data|date=14 January 2019|website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>

The current publicly available annual National Health Interview Survey data release consists of four files which describe the demographics and health-related characteristics of the survey population at the household, family, and person-level, as well as two files designed to capture information on any injuries experienced during the year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/nhis_2010_data_release.htm|title=NHIS – 2010 Data Release|date=10 May 2019|website=www.cdc.gov}}</ref>

=== Core ===

==== Household File ====

With one record per household in the sample, this file mainly contains descriptors necessary to determine the number of individuals and families within each sampled household, and allows researchers to link families or other unrelated individuals captured in any of the other Core files based on household of residence (using the HHX variable).  This file also contains basic information on non-response and a household-level final weight.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2010/househld_summary.pdf |title=Health statistics |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

==== Family File ====

This file contains one record per family in the sample, with general information on identifiers (such as family member age, race, family structure, family income), health status and limitations, injuries and poisonings, access to care and utilization, and health insurance.  The family file can be linked to other files containing information on adults and children within each family (using the HHX and FMX variables).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Survey_Questionnaires/NHIS/2010/2010_Q_Reference_Guide.pdf |title=Survey questions |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

==== Person File ====

This file contains information on every individual within every family within every household selected for participation in the NHIS.  Survey data about individuals who were either not available at the time of the interview or under 18 were provided by an available adult in the household.  This person-level file contains information on health status and limitation of activity, health care access and utilization, health insurance, socio-demographics, and income and assets.  Examining this file using the final weight variable (WTFA) generalizes to the entire noninstitutional, civilian United States population.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2010/personsx_summary.pdf |title=Health statistics |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

==== Sample Adult and Sample Child Files ====

These two files contain information obtained from the survey response of one adult and one child (if one exists) sampled from each family contained in the family file, and can be linked up to household and family information (using the HHX and FMX variables).  These two sample person files contain much more in-depth information about health conditions, physical and mental health status, health limitations, behaviors, and utilization than the family file.  Their question topics are specific to either adults or children, but not both (such as occupational demographic questions in the adult file and childhood immunization questions in the child file).{{cn|date=March 2024}}

Much like the Person file, these two files can be used to create national estimates of all adults and children in the United States (using WTFA_SA to generalize to all adults and WTFA_SC to generalize to all children).  Individuals can be matched between the Person and Sample Adult/Child files using the HHX (household), FMX (family), and FPX (person) fields.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2010/srvydesc.pdf |title=Health Statistics |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

==== Injury and Poisoning Files ====

The Injury and Poisoning Episode file contains event-level information about any injury event experienced by an individual within the household in the three months leading up to the interview.  For each reported injury or poisoning event, a number of questions examining the severity and effect of the event were asked, such as whether a physician was consulted and what kind of injury was experienced.  This episode file can be used to generalize about the frequency of all injuries experienced by Americans over a defined window of time.  The final weight (WTFA) generalizes to the number of injuries that occur among the U.S. population.  This file can be merged on to any of the other data files using the HHX (household), FMX (family), and FPX (person) merge fields.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2010/injpoiep_layout.pdf |title=Health Statistics |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

The Injury and Poisoning Verbatim file contains un-categorized, open-ended data provided by the respondent.  This file can be linked to the cleaned Episode file using the HHX, FMX, FPX, and IPEPNO (Injury/Poisoning Episode Number) fields.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2010/injverbt_summary.pdf |title=Health Statistics |date=2010 |website=ftp.cdc.gov |access-date=2019-06-11}}</ref>

=== Supplemental ===

Supplemental data are available whenever funding and sponsorship allow. The topics of non-core questionnaires generally relate to a matter of current importance to policymakers or the research community.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

'''Occupational Health Supplement'''

In 2010 and 2015, supplemental data were collected that relate to the impacts of work on health. Known as the Occupational Health Supplements, these data are available to chart using the Worker Health Charts tool. Worker Health Charts is a tool NIOSH uses to allow the public to visualize NHIS data, along with other work-related data sources. See the CDC Feature on Worker Health Charts and the NIOSH Science Blog to learn more about the tool and how it works.{{cn|date=March 2024}}
